title: Match Messaging Volume Critique
scenario: The BooedUp product team recently shipped a new Match recommendation surface to help users discover high Type Score candidates faster. The team wants to measure whether messaging engagement improved.
prompt: The product manager proposes tracking 'Total Messages Sent by Users with at Least One Match' as the key success metric for the new Match recommendation surface. The PM argues this metric shows whether users are more engaged in conversations after the feature launched. What is wrong with this metric as stated? Propose a better metric.
instructions: One short sentence: name the flaw, propose a fix. Example answer length: 'Should be normalized. Messages per Match is better.' No formulas required.
proposed_metric: Total Messages Sent by Users with at Least One Match
stakeholder_rationale: Shows users are more engaged in conversations after the new recommendation surface shipped.

numerator.label: Total messages sent by users with at least one Match
First messages sent after a Match connection
Messages sent in the first 24 hours after Match

denominator.label: Match connections established in the period
Users with at least one Match
Profile views that led to Match

metric_movers.reason: Population size grew or shrank (e.g., viral TikTok post drove signups, inflating total message volume)
metric_movers.explanation: More users with at least one Match sends more total messages even if per-Match engagement stayed flat.

metric_movers.reason: Per-pair Match quality changed (e.g., Match Score algorithm regressed, lowering messages per pair)
metric_movers.explanation: Lower quality Matches send fewer messages per pair, even if total Matches increased.

metric_movers.reason: Mix of relationship types shifted (e.g., more users transitioned Match to Wingman, reducing Match message volume)
metric_movers.explanation: Wingman messaging is not counted, so a shift away from Match relationships lowers the numerator.

metric_movers.reason: Measurement definition changed (e.g., event tracking excluded messages sent via Cloud Functions retry)
metric_movers.explanation: If some messages were previously double-counted or now undercounted, the metric moves without real user behavior change.

metric_movers.reason: External platform policy changed (e.g., iOS push notification permission rate dropped, reducing message open rate)
metric_movers.explanation: Fewer push notifications delivered means users miss Match messages, lowering total sent.

metric_movers.reason: Premium tier pricing increased (e.g., $9.99 to $12.99), changing Premium subscriber mix
metric_movers.explanation: Premium pricing affects subscription conversion but does not directly move total messages sent by Match users.

metric_movers.reason: Speed dating event promotion launched (e.g., homepage banner drove RSVPs)
metric_movers.explanation: Event RSVPs are a separate flow and do not directly affect Match messaging volume.

metric_movers.reason: Profile photo verification step redesigned (e.g., new UI reduced friction in signup funnel)
metric_movers.explanation: Verification happens before users can Match, so it affects activation but not messaging per existing Match.

expected_themes: not normalized per Match or per user
messages per Match is the fix
reference_answer: Should be normalized per Match. Messages per Match is better, since total message volume can grow just from more users signing up, not from better engagement per Match.

grading_rubric.description: Names that the metric is a raw count not normalized per Match connection or per user with a Match
Notes that total messages can increase due to more users or more Matches, not better per-Match engagement
Suggests a per-Match or per-user rate (e.g., Messages per Match, Messages per User with Match)
Answer is one to two sentences, not padded with generic commentary

hints: Think about what happens if the number of users with Matches doubles but each Match sends the same number of messages.
The metric is a total count. What kind of metric would isolate per-Match engagement?
The flaw is that the metric does not normalize. What would you divide by to make it a rate?
common_mistakes: Saying the metric is 'vanity' without naming the normalization flaw
Proposing a counter-metric instead of fixing the proposed metric
Focusing on message quality (response rate, conversation depth) when the core flaw is the lack of a denominator
Writing a long explanation instead of a one-sentence critique
